topics: Causes of the First World War

data.sourceTitle: Causes of the First World War
data.targetTitle: Causes of the First World War
data.sourcePassage:
The First World War broke out in 1914 because of a combination of long-term tensions and a short-term trigger. Historians often group the long-term causes under four headings: militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism. Before 1914, many European powers built up large armies and navies. Germany greatly expanded its military, which worried Britain because Britain depended on sea power to protect its island and empire. European countries also formed alliance systems. The Triple Alliance linked Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy, while the Triple Entente linked Britain, France and Russia. These alliances meant that a local crisis could spread into a wider war.

The short-term trigger was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. He was shot by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and issued a harsh ultimatum. When Serbia did not agree to all the terms, Austria-Hungary declared war. The alliance system then pulled in other countries. Germany supported Austria-Hungary. Russia supported Serbia and mobilised its army. Germany declared war on Russia and France, then invaded Belgium. Britain had agreed to protect Belgian neutrality in 1839 and declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914. The assassination alone did not cause the war. Without the long-term tensions already present in Europe, the crisis might have been contained.

questions.question: Where was Archduke Franz Ferdinand assassinated?
questions.modelAnswer: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.

questions.question: Which countries were linked by the Triple Entente?
questions.modelAnswer: The Triple Entente linked Britain, France and Russia.

questions.question: Why did Britain declare war on Germany in August 1914?
options: Germany invaded neutral Belgium and Britain had agreed to protect it
Britain was part of the Triple Alliance
questions.modelAnswer: Britain declared war because Germany invaded Belgium. Britain had agreed in 1839 to protect Belgian neutrality.

questions.question: Why is it historically inaccurate to say that the assassination alone caused the First World War?
options: Because the assassination never actually happened
Because only Germany caused the war
Because long-term tensions such as militarism and alliances already made Europe unstable
Because Britain declared war before the assassination
questions.modelAnswer: The assassination was a trigger, but Europe was already tense due to militarism, alliances, imperialism and nationalism. Without these long-term factors, the crisis might not have become a world war.

data.sourcePassage:
After Germany's advance was halted at the First Battle of the Marne in 1914, both sides dug into the ground along a line stretching from the English Channel to the Swiss border. This became known as the Western Front. The result was stalemate: neither side could break through the other's defences for much of the war.

Trench life was difficult and dangerous. Soldiers dealt with mud, cold, damp, lice, rats and the constant threat of shellfire. Machine guns made open attacks across no man's land extremely dangerous. Barbed wire slowed attackers, and defenders had a significant advantage. However, soldiers did not spend all their time in the front-line trench. They rotated between front-line trenches, support trenches, reserve areas and rest camps.

New weapons changed the nature of warfare. Poison gas was first used on a large scale in 1915, causing fear and injury. Tanks were introduced by the British at the Battle of the Somme in 1916. Early tanks were slow and unreliable, but they showed that it was possible to cross trenches and barbed wire. Aircraft were used for reconnaissance, helping armies observe enemy positions and direct artillery fire. Despite these technological developments, stalemate continued for much of the war. It was only in 1918, when combined tactics using tanks, artillery, aircraft and infantry were used together more effectively, that the Allies began to break through German lines.

questions.question: What was the name given to the main fighting area in Belgium and northern France?
questions.modelAnswer: The main fighting area in Belgium and northern France was called the Western Front.

questions.question: In which battle were tanks first used by the British?
questions.modelAnswer: Tanks were first used by the British at the Battle of the Somme in 1916.

questions.question: Why did trench warfare create a stalemate on the Western Front?
options: Both sides ran out of ammunition immediately
Machine guns, barbed wire and trenches gave defenders a strong advantage over attackers
Both armies agreed not to advance
questions.modelAnswer: Machine guns made open attacks extremely dangerous, and barbed wire slowed attackers. Defenders in trenches had a strong advantage, making it very difficult for either side to break through.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to say that all soldiers spent four years in front-line trenches?
options: Because soldiers never went to the trenches at all
Because soldiers rotated between front-line, support and reserve trenches as well as rest camps
Because the war only lasted one year
Because only officers went to trenches
questions.modelAnswer: Soldiers moved between front-line trenches, support trenches, reserve areas and rest camps. Experiences varied widely depending on role, rank, timing and location.

topics: Consequences of the First World War

data.sourceTitle: The Consequences of the First World War
data.targetTitle: The Consequences of the First World War
data.sourcePassage:
The First World War ended with an armistice at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918. Fighting stopped, but the peace settlement still had to be decided. In 1919, the Treaty of Versailles was signed. Germany was blamed for causing the war under Article 231, known as the war guilt clause. Germany had to pay reparations to the Allies, reduce its army to 100,000 soldiers, give up territory, and was forbidden from uniting with Austria. The Rhineland near France was demilitarised. These terms created deep resentment in Germany. Many Germans called the treaty a Diktat, meaning a dictated peace imposed without negotiation.

The war had enormous human and economic costs. Millions of soldiers and civilians died across Europe and beyond. The British Empire lost around 900,000 military personnel. The conflict stretched across the world, involving troops from India, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the Caribbean, Africa and many other parts of the British Empire.

After the war, communities built war memorials and held remembrance ceremonies. The poppy became a symbol of loss after the poem 'In Flanders Fields'. However, the meaning of the war remained contested. Some focused on sacrifice and service, others on tragedy and waste, and others on the global dimensions of the conflict that official memory often overlooked. The Treaty of Versailles contributed to later tensions in Europe, though the Second World War had many causes and a simple link between the two wars should be avoided.

questions.question: What was the name given to Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles?
questions.modelAnswer: Article 231 was known as the war guilt clause. It blamed Germany and its allies for causing the war.

questions.question: Approximately how many military personnel did the British Empire lose in the First World War?
questions.modelAnswer: The British Empire lost around 900,000 military personnel during the First World War.

questions.question: Why did many Germans resent the Treaty of Versailles?
options: Because it gave Germany more land than before
Because Germany was not allowed to keep its navy
Because the terms were seen as a humiliating dictated peace that blamed Germany unfairly
Because the League of Nations admitted Germany immediately
questions.modelAnswer: Many Germans resented the treaty because they had not been invited to negotiate, and the terms — including war guilt, reparations and military limits — were seen as deeply humiliating.

questions.question: Why should historians avoid saying that the Treaty of Versailles directly caused the Second World War?
options: Because the treaty had no effect at all
Because the Second World War had many causes and a simple one-cause explanation is inaccurate
Because Germany accepted the treaty willingly
questions.modelAnswer: The Treaty of Versailles contributed to later tensions in Europe, but the Second World War had many causes including the Great Depression, the rise of Hitler, appeasement and German expansionism. Reducing complex historical events to one cause oversimplifies the past.
